title: But My Students Like Written Comments...
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Following her earlier post on the limits of written feedback, Daisy Christodoulou argues that no amount of additional detail rescues written comments, because prose simply isn't the right medium for changing student performance. Using an extended driving-instructor analogy -- a lengthy, accurate, detailed written comment about parallel parking is still far less useful than another attempt at parallel parking focused on the specific fix needed -- she argues students need practice and action, not more elaborate description of their errors. Her preferred alternative is whole-class feedback: rather than writing individual comments, a teacher reviews all student responses, notes common errors, and plans a targeted lesson or sequence addressing them directly. She acknowledges the practical and cultural resistance to dropping written comments entirely -- students, parents, and senior leaders often treat visible ink in a book as a proxy for teacher effort and quality -- and proposes AI as a way to resolve the tension: at No More Marking, teachers now record short verbal comments during Comparative Judgement sessions, which AI transcribes and turns into individual feedback, whole-class reports, and even year-group and national-level reports.
points: Christodoulou's driving-instructor analogy makes an abstract feedback-theory argument viscerally concrete: even a maximally detailed, accurate written comment cannot substitute for another attempt at the actual skill.

Her core proposed mechanism -- extending a comment's length or detail doesn't fix its usefulness, because the problem is the medium (prose) not the content -- reframes 'better feedback' away from writing more and toward practising more.

She names the specific social pressure keeping written comments alive despite their weak evidence base: parents and senior leaders treat visible ink in a book as a proxy for teacher commitment, independent of whether it actually helps students.

Her AI-assisted system (verbal comments during judgement sessions, transcribed and turned into individual and whole-class reports) is a concrete existing product, not a hypothetical future tool, giving the piece a real implementation to point to.
quotes: If a student gets a comment in their exercise book that says “you need to be more systematic” or “you need to infer more insightfully”, how is that going to help them improve?
Written comments like this might be true, but they aren’t useful. They are like a thermometer, in that they tell you a student’s weaknesses.
I think that prose is just not the most effective medium if you want to help a student improve.
Students and parents like seeing the teachers’ writing in books and feel it’s a sign of personal attention - even though a teacher may end up writing the exact same thing in dozens of books.
The reason, of course, is that written comments are incredibly time-consuming. But this is where AI might be able to help.

The AI transcribes all of the verbal comments from all of the teachers. The AI turns these comments into a) individual written feedback for each student b) a whole class feedback report for the class teacher.
In our initial trials, this system sped up the production of both student feedback and whole-class feedback.
